channel.title: Personal News Feed — News & World Affairs
channel.description: Personally scored news, world affairs, opinion/analysis & foreign affairs, business & finance, and San Diego/local articles curated by news-filter

item.title: Global brain cell mapping advances dementia treatments
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Science Original headline: Brain cell mapping lays groundwork for better treatments for conditions like dementia
Scientists mapped the basal ganglia, a brain region critical for movement and disease, using data from humans, macaques, and marmosets. The atlas, created by researchers at the Allen Institute and over 50 institutions, details 25 million cells, their gene expression, and differences across species. It includes a 3D map with gene activity layers linked to diseases like Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. Researchers say the tool could help develop targeted treatments with fewer side effects, such as for Parkinson's. The project, funded by the National Institutes of Health, aims to expand the atlas to the entire brain by 2024. Satrajit Ghosh compared the effort to the Human Genome Project, while Talia Lerner highlighted potential for improving therapies. The work provides a framework for future brain research, with methods and collaborations expected to accelerate progress.

item.title: CDC reports rising flu cases; experts urge pre-travel vaccination
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: More people are getting the flu. Should you get a flu shot before you travel?
CDC reports rising flu cases; experts urge pre-travel vaccination. More people are contracting influenza this fall, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Dr. William Schaffner warns that the flu started earlier this year and is spreading, advising travelers to get vaccinated before Thanksgiving. The flu shot takes about ten days to reach full efficacy, leaving time for vaccination. With 82 million people expected to travel over 50 miles during Thanksgiving, gathering in enclosed spaces increases transmission risk. Vaccination reduces hospitalization risks from complications like pneumonia, especially for seniors, children, and those with underlying conditions. Schaffner also notes low COVID booster rates, stressing that vaccines remain critical for preventing severe illness. Claire Hannan of the Association of Immunization Managers confirms vaccines for flu, COVID, and RSV are widely available, urging prompt vaccination as influenza circulates and holidays approach.

item.title: The 10 states set to build the least housing in the coming years
item.description:
Source: Business Insider
The Lied Center for Real Estate report shows U.S. housing permits per 1,000 residents averaged 2.83 from January to August 2026. States lagging behind this rate risk higher housing prices as demand outpaces supply. Alaska had the lowest permit rate at 0.72, 75% below the national average, with a 12.3% decline from 2023. Connecticut ranked second-lowest at 3,799 permits, 64% below the national rate, and performed poorly across four metrics. Nevada, Alaska, Connecticut, North Dakota, and Maryland all struggled across multiple metrics. West Virginia ranked 10th-lowest at 1.55 permits per 1,000 residents, 45% below the average, but its permit pace outpaced projected household growth due to shrinking households. Nicholas Irwin, report coauthor, warned that insufficient permits exacerbate affordability issues. He emphasized the need to build more housing across all types to meet demand.

item.title: San Diego Approves Fewer New Homes, ADUs and Moderate-Income Units Rise
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: San Diego OKs fewer new homes for second year in row, but ADUs and moderate-income units surge
San Diego approved 7,630 new homes in 2025, down from 8,782 in 2024 and 9,693 in 2023, missing state goals for 2029. ADUs accounted for 28% of new units, up from 26% in 2024, with North Park leading approvals. The city is still underproducing in high-resource areas, where 36% of units were approved despite those areas comprising 61% of the city. Moderate-income housing rose to 620 units in 2025, driven by ADU incentives, though 295 were ADUs. Larger family housing remains low, with only 13% of units having three or more bedrooms. Heidi Vonblum cited economic slowdowns and rising costs as reasons for the decline. ADU approvals surged due to incentives allowing one market-rate unit per rent-restricted unit, but the policy is being rolled back. The city’s 2023 peak of 9,693 units made state targets seem achievable, but 2024-2025 numbers now leave a 71,503-unit gap by 2029.

item.title: U.S. Tightens Chip Export Rules to Block China's Remote Access
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Business, BBC News Original headline: US Tightens Chip Export Rules to Block China's Remote Access
The U.S. Commerce Department announced new export rules to block China from accessing advanced computer chips via third-country data centers. The regulations target nations like Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Singapore, and Brazil, aiming to close a loophole where Chinese entities could indirectly benefit by renting computing power through overseas facilities. Critics argue existing rules allowed this by permitting chip sales to foreign data centers, which could be accessed remotely by Chinese firms. Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center operator and largest Nvidia chip buyer in Southeast Asia, denies smuggling allegations, stating its operations are 'legitimate and lawful.' The company noted former director Alice Huang, linked to Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang, left over a year ago. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned current regulations are insufficient to prevent China from leveraging remote computing for AI development. The rules, drafted by Treasury and the National Security Council, aim to curb China's tech access, with the Institute for Progress projecting 30% of China's advanced AI computing power could come from overseas rentals by 2027. China's foreign ministry called the restrictions 'economic coercion,' while Southeast Asian nations face balancing data center investments with stricter export controls.

item.title: Berkshire Hathaway Adjusts Stock Portfolio in Buffett's Final Weeks as Chairman
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Berkshire Hathaway bought and sold these stocks during Warren Buffett's final weeks as chairman
Berkshire Hathaway made minor portfolio adjustments during Warren Buffett's final weeks as chairman. Regulatory filings show the company reduced positions in Capital One, VeriSign, Nucor, and Kroger, while increasing stakes in Delta Air Lines and Lennar. The firm also added a small stake in Bending Spoons. Buffett noted his involvement in Alphabet's investment, now worth $36 billion. The changes occurred alongside Buffett's announcement of a $5.5 billion donation to family foundations. Berkshire's third-quarter stock purchases totaled $2.4 billion, with $9.6 billion spent on buybacks. The company's share price rose 19% since October, reaching $593. Buffett, who stepped down as chairman in September, faced challenges finding bargains as valuations rose, leading to quiet portfolio activity.

item.title: Caltrans presents options for repairing Ramona sidewalks affected by eucalyptus trees
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune
Caltrans presented seven options for repairing sidewalks along state Route 67/Main Street in Ramona, damaged by eucalyptus tree roots. A November 12 meeting at the Ramona Library received favorable feedback on alternatives A (natural trail), C (relocate sidewalk outside tree line), and D (flexible materials). Options involving tree removal or roadway elevation were eliminated. Steve Welborn noted the southbound sidewalk remains in good condition, while northbound roots require more extensive work. Karina Cantero-Angel outlined next steps, including a public engagement plan and environmental study. Funding will come from Proposition 1B. Maintenance crews are currently grinding root-caused sidewalk lifts. A future public meeting will finalize preferred alternatives.

item.title: Japan, South Korea, Taiwan Respond to Suspected Russian Air Incursions
item.description:
Source: BBC News, Deutsche Welle Original headline: Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan Respond to Suspected Russian Air Incursions
Japan scrambled fighter jets after two suspected Russian aircraft entered its airspace near Okinoshima island, prompting a 'very stern protest' from Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara. The planes flew through the Tsushima Strait and near Yonaguni Island before heading toward the Pacific, following a similar 2024 incident. Japan's actions come amid tensions with Russia, which detained a Japanese journalist and seized assets from Japanese companies. South Korea deployed jets after unspecified Russian military aircraft entered its air defense identification zone over the Sea of Japan, though airspace was not violated. Taiwan reported responding to Russian aircraft in its own zone. Overlapping air defense zones in the East China Sea involve China, Taiwan, Japan, and South Korea. Foreign military aircraft are not legally required to notify governments before entering such zones. The incidents occur amid broader tensions, including Russia's Apec summit participation and Japan's sanctions against Moscow over Ukraine. Russia has not commented on the allegations, leaving implications for regional stability unresolved.

item.title: United Airlines Resolves Tech Outage Causing Flight Delays
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune, Business Insider, Deutsche Welle Original headline: United Airlines Resolves Technology Outage Causing Flight Delays Amid Recent Tech Disruptions
United Airlines resolved a technology outage that delayed hundreds of flights on Monday. The issue, lasting over 90 minutes, disrupted flight operations but did not affect aircraft in the air or United Express flights. Pilots reported problems with a system calculating an aircraft’s final weight before takeoff, critical for safe departure. The airline fixed the problem approximately 1 hour and 40 minutes after initial reports. United apologized to passengers via social media. Flight tracking service FlightAware listed around 600 delayed flights, though the exact number tied to the outage remained unclear. The incident followed a FAA ground stop on Friday due to air traffic control system failures, which were unrelated to cybersecurity or AI. United’s outage occurred days after a similar system failure in August 2025, which grounded planes at major U.S. airports. The airline did not confirm if the same system was affected. Other recent tech failures included JPMorgan’s software bug and Microsoft’s widespread outage. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo praised United for prioritizing safety by delaying flights. The FAA’s ground stop and United’s outage highlight vulnerabilities in aviation technology, as noted by Deutsche Welle.
item.source: San Diego Union-Tribune, Business Insider, Deutsche Welle

item.title: San Diego Flights Resume After FAA Ground Stop Ends
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: San Diego flights stabilize following historic national FAA ground stop
San Diego flights resumed normal operations after the FAA ended a four-hour nationwide ground stop. The shutdown, the second such event since 9/11, disrupted schedules with 364 delays and 48 cancellations at San Diego International Airport. The crisis stemmed from a telecommunications upgrade at L3Harris in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a faulty router caused 1,000 connection attempts per four to five seconds, overwhelming 17 air traffic control centers. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed disabling 69 routers resolved the issue. Officials dismissed foreign cyberattack theories and linked the outage to legacy hardware, not the new SMART AI tool. The incident reignited debates over U.S. aviation infrastructure, with officials urging emergency funding for modernization. Travelers are advised to check airline updates for real-time changes.

item.title: U.N. Talks Seek to Rein in 'Killer Robots' Amid AI Weapon Fears
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: U.N. talks seek to rein in 'killer robots' as fears over AI weapons grow
U.N. negotiations on lethal autonomous weapons, known as 'killer robots,' are underway in Geneva. Supporters argue this is the last chance to establish rules before autonomous weapons can make kill decisions without human oversight. Experts warn rapid advancements in warfare technology could soon enable weapons to target and eliminate individuals autonomously. In Ukraine and Gaza, AI-assisted weapons have been used, but they remain under human control. Humanitarian groups insist the decision to kill must stay in human hands. The U.N., International Committee of the Red Cross, and Pope have called for legally binding rules, with U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warning that fully autonomous weapons would cross a 'moral red line.' The Red Cross fears existing Geneva Conventions cannot be upheld by autonomous systems, citing risks of misidentifying targets. Georgia Haines, a Red Cross legal adviser, stated autonomous weapons lack the contextual understanding humans possess, increasing misidentification risks. Human rights groups warn AI-assisted weapons could proliferate to non-state actors, enabling targeted attacks based on arbitrary criteria. At least 50 countries, including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, and Germany, support strict timelines for binding rules. The U.S., Russia, and Israel oppose legally binding frameworks, preferring non-binding guidelines. The U.S. has historically resisted international treaties, such as the Ottawa Convention on landmines. A compromise may involve extending negotiations for states to adopt rules as binding or non-binding, though campaigners view this as delaying critical action.

item.title: Brokerage Features Highlighted for 2027 Include AI Trading and Free Funds
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Original headline: 5 Brokerage Features We’re Excited for in 2027 (And 2 Things We Could Do Without)
NerdWallet's investing team tested over 15 brokerage accounts in 2026, evaluating features like AI trading tools, fee structures, and cash management. AI-driven agents, such as Public's 'Agents' and Robinhood's Cortex, allow users to execute trades via natural language, with Public offering automated strategies and cash sweeps. Fidelity and E*TRADE introduced no-expense-ratio index funds, making investing more accessible. Robinhood and Public provide competitive interest rates on uninvested cash, with Public's base rate at 3.3% and Robinhood's premium offering 3.75%. Direct indexing, once costly, is now available through online brokers for tax optimization and ethical investing. The team expressed caution about AI-driven portfolio advice accountability and the potential for free funds to prioritize user acquisition over pure investment value. These features and concerns highlight evolving trends in brokerage innovation and user priorities.

item.title: Mortgage Rates Rise Slightly to 7.27%
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Original headline: Mortgage Rates Today, Monday, November 16: A Little Higher
Mortgage rates rose slightly to 7.27% APR for a 30-year fixed-rate loan, up 37 basis points from a week ago. The increase follows mixed inflation data from the October Producer Price Index, which showed 0.3% monthly price growth but 6.5% year-over-year inflation. Investors expect the Federal Reserve to raise borrowing rates in December, which typically drives up mortgage rates. NerdWallet advises refinancing if current rates are at least 0.5-0.75 percentage points lower than existing rates, especially for those with rates above 7.76%. Factors like credit scores, down payments, and financial profiles influence personalized rate quotes. Lenders adjust rates frequently, so locking in a rate offers protection against market fluctuations. Preapproval and comparing lender offers are recommended to secure a mortgage at today’s rates.

item.title: Landfill gas release triggers evacuations in Santa Clarita Valley
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Dark smoke at the Chiquita Canyon Landfill in Santa Clarita Valley prompts evacuations
Dark smoke and a reported gas release at the Chiquita Canyon Landfill prompted evacuations in Santa Clarita Valley. The incident occurred at 4:04 p.m. on Monday, according to Lt. Brendan Kinsella of the Santa Clarita sheriff’s station. Six landfill workers were hospitalized with minor injuries after crews conducting routine digging encountered a gas deposit, said Inspector Jonathan Torres of the L.A. County Fire Department. A hazmat team was dispatched, and the situation is now deemed static with no health risks, per Fire Department testing. The city issued evacuation advisories for zones CAS-VALVERDE-A, CAS-HASLEY, CAS-HILLCREST, CAS-CAMBRIDGE, and CAS-INDUSTRY, warning residents to prepare for potential evacuation. The South Coast Air Quality Management District had not issued an air quality advisory by 6 p.m. Torres could not confirm an explosion, though a fire captain was en route to the scene.

item.title: Illumina to Lay Off 51 San Diego Employees Amid Cost-Cutting
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Illumina announces layoffs at San Diego headquarters
Illumina announced plans to lay off 51 employees at its San Diego headquarters, effective Nov. 9 through Jan. 8. The cuts span managerial, lab technician, engineer, and scientist roles, per a WARN notice. The company, a major biotech employer, faces ongoing financial pressures from federal research funding cuts, tariffs, and trade tensions with China. Illumina’s third-quarter sales rose 4.16% year-over-year to $1.13 billion, with a 47% increase in profit to $220 million. However, China’s Unreliable Entity List blacklist, imposed in early 2025, reduced revenue from the country to 5% of sales, down from 10% in 2022. CEO Jacob Thaysen acknowledged the challenge, stating the company is focused on mitigating its impact. Shares closed Monday at $198, down 3.5% despite a 47.4% year-to-date gain. The state reports San Diego employee count between 1,000 and 4,999, though Illumina does not break down headcount by facility.

item.title: La Jolla resident turns to Town Council to discuss possible Prospect Place traffic fixes
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune
La Jolla resident Brad Schnell presented a proposal to the Town Council on Nov. 12 to address traffic safety concerns on Prospect Place. He described the five-way intersection near The Village as resembling a 'drag strip' at night, with drivers frequently exceeding speed limits. Schnell cited an incident where his car was damaged by a driver going over 70 mph. His plan includes establishing a crosswalk at Park Row, restriping the street, and adding bollards to direct traffic. He also used an AI simulation to model traffic patterns during peak hours and under challenging lighting conditions. The proposal was not subject to a vote and will be reviewed by the La Jolla Traffic & Transportation Board. Schnell previously sought a city study through the Get It Done app but aimed for more comprehensive data collection. The Town Council meeting concluded with holiday safety tips from San Diego first responders and information about an anticipated strong El Niño event.

item.title: Corporate Fleets Drive EV Adoption Despite Low Consumer Interest
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Original headline: The EV Boom Is Happening Without Car Buyers
Corporate fleets and businesses are driving the electric vehicle (EV) boom despite low consumer interest. Amazon, USPS, FedEx, IKEA, and others are adopting EVs for delivery and logistics, with Amazon using 50,000 Rivian vans. Robotaxis now operate in 12 cities, and 10% of Uber miles in the U.S. and Canada are zero-emission. Jeremy Michalek of Carnegie Mellon notes that businesses prioritize cost savings: EVs are cheaper to operate due to lower maintenance and fuel costs, especially for high-mileage vehicles. Companies like Rivian and Uber are expanding EV fleets, with Rivian securing a $1 billion deal for 50,000 robotaxis. Tech firms like Waymo and Hyundai are also investing in EVs for autonomous systems. While long-haul trucks and infrastructure remain challenges, corporate adoption is boosting the industry. Despite most EV makers being unprofitable, fleet demand provides stability. Until consumer adoption grows, businesses will shape the EV market's future.

item.title: Africa Shifts Toward Using Yuan in Trade
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World Original headline: Africa: Trading in yuan
Zambia becomes first African nation to accept yuan for mine taxes and royalties, signaling a shift from dollar dominance. China, Africa's largest trading partner, is driving increased use of the yuan for trade and debt payments. Experts note the trend could reduce dollar reliance in commodity sectors like lithium, copper, and cobalt. Kenya and other countries have restructured debt to China using yuan. African banks now offer direct yuan transactions, reducing conversion costs. While U.S. tariffs encourage diversification, analysts say rapid dollar replacement is unlikely. Instead, a gradual shift toward multiple currencies is underway, with the yuan gaining traction but not displacing the dollar immediately.

item.title: JPMorgan Chase Software Bug Causes Online Banking Delays
item.description:
Source: Business Insider, San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: JPMorgan Chase Software Bug Causes Widespread Online Banking Delays
JPMorgan Chase's software bug disrupted online banking services, causing transaction delays and access issues for customers of major U.S. banks and Zelle. The bank attributed the problem to an on-premise hardware system issue, not cybersecurity, and said it resolved the problem by the end of the day. Chase's spokesperson, Joe Evangelisti, stated other banks' systems were not directly impacted, though some experienced transaction slowness due to interactions with Chase. Customers at Bank of America, Wells Fargo, US Bank, and Capital One reported issues, per DownDetector.com. Capital One confirmed its systems were unaffected, while US Bank noted potential delays for Zelle payments. Zelle, owned by Early Warning Services, remained operational but some customers faced delays due to the Chase glitch. Chase emphasized the issue was isolated and not a systemic problem, with no evidence of malicious activity. The incident followed unrelated technical outages, including Microsoft and FAA failures. Chase's latest statement on November 16, 2026, reiterated the problem was a software bug, not a cyberattack.

item.title: National City Council Considers Tax Plan Falling Short of Revenue Goal
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: National City council to weigh business-backed tax plan that falls short of initial revenue goal
National City Council will consider a business-backed tax plan that would raise business license taxes by 0.07% on annual gross receipts, a $100 fee, and a $30,000 cap, generating $2.73 million annually—$2.27 million below the $5 million goal. Staff recommends evaluating higher-revenue models, including $40,000 cap proposals projected to raise $5.65 million and $5.85 million. The city faces a $13 million deficit, with potential insolvency by 2030 if no action is taken. A special election to approve a tax measure would cost at least $350,000 and require a fiscal emergency declaration. Councilmembers will change after Dec. 8, with incoming members deciding the tax plan. Councilmember Jose Rodriguez said the new council should govern, while Mayor Ron Morrison called the business-backed plan ‘progress’ but warned it would raise costs by 300% for businesses. A separate citizens’ initiative aims to raise $10.5 million via a 2028 ballot measure.

item.title: Walnut High School Lockdown Suspected Swatting After Gun and Bomb Reports
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Walnut High School locked down after reports of gun and bomb. 'Swatting' suspected
Walnut High School locked down Monday after a 911 call reported an armed individual with a bomb on campus. Sheriff’s deputies responded to the school on 400 N. Pierre Road, but found no weapons. Deputy Kari Mercer said the call likely was a 'swatting' attempt, a hoax involving false threats. A student was detained during the lockdown but was not immediately released or arrested. Law enforcement agencies have faced similar hoax calls in the past, including incidents at hospitals, places of worship, and celebrity homes. The city of Walnut confirmed no threat to the area but kept deputies on scene. Mercer noted the call described the student as armed with a bomb and gun, but no weapons were located.

item.title: Japan’s Defense Reforms Draw Lessons From Ukraine and Middle East Conflicts
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Original headline: Japan’s Defense Lessons From Ukraine and the Middle East
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has revised defense policies to address prolonged conflicts, raising security spending to 1.8% of GDP by 2025-2026. The Defense Ministry emphasizes domestic production capacity as critical to deterrence, citing lessons from Ukraine and the Middle East. Analysts note that modern warfare requires sustained resource allocation, shifting focus from quick campaigns to long-term operations. Japan’s strategy includes expanding defense industrial capacity, with plans for new subsidies and government-owned contractor facilities to boost wartime production. However, challenges persist: insufficient parts production limits equipment availability, and the supply chain remains vulnerable, with over 11,000 manufacturers involved in defense systems. Tokyo is exploring foreign maintenance partnerships with Australia and Indonesia to enhance resilience. Despite reforms, legal gaps hinder wartime production control, and the government faces questions about translating peacetime capacity into combat readiness. Upcoming policy revisions aim to clarify wartime authority over civilian manufacturers and strengthen deterrence through strategic communication.

item.title: Motorcyclist caught speeding at 136 mph by CHP
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Motorcyclist speeding at 136 mph is pulled over by CHP
A motorcyclist was stopped by California Highway Patrol officers for speeding at 136 mph on the 101 Freeway near Santa Barbara Airport. CHP shared a radar reading photo showing the excessive speed, noting that such velocity leaves little reaction time for hazards and increases crash severity. The rider, wearing blue jeans and a sweatshirt, received a ticket for exceeding the speed limit by more than double. CHP emphasized motorcyclists face higher injury risks in accidents compared to car occupants. Los Angeles recently deployed speed cameras at busy intersections, with a test on Pacific Coast Highway capturing 100,000 violations over nine days.

item.title: Melbourne Cup Horse's Body Found in Sydney Skip Bin
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Body of Melbourne Cup horse found dumped in Sydney skip
The body of a top Australian racehorse, So You Are, was found dumped in a skip bin in Sydney, hours after its trainer revealed the horse had died from colic. Trainer Bjorn Baker expressed distress over the video showing the horse's remains in a bin surrounded by rubbish, calling for a full explanation. Racing NSW stated the horse was later properly buried but condemned the handling as 'completely unacceptable.' The five-year-old had won four races in spring, including the Bendigo Cup, before finishing eighth in the Melbourne Cup. The horse was euthanized after a severe colic episode and transported for burial. A contractor hired by REC Equine Specialists, the hospital where the horse died, disposed of the body, though the company apologized and stopped using the contractor. The landfill site confirmed the body was placed in a permitted area, but the incident has sparked criticism over animal remains handling protocols. Racing NSW emphasized that burial at a licensed landfill is standard for euthanized animals but should be done respectfully and promptly.

item.title: Ukraine Strikes Kerch Bridge as Aerial Warfare Escalates
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News, Deutsche Welle Original headline: Ukraine Strikes Key Crimea Bridge as Aerial Warfare Escalates
Ukraine launched a major strike on the Kerch Bridge, a key link between Russia and Crimea, using drones and missiles over several weeks. President Zelenskyy called the operation 'unprecedented,' targeting both road and rail sections, with part of the bridge collapsing. Russian officials confirmed damage but claimed movement across the bridge was halted without specifying the extent. Russia's Investigative Committee stated the bridge was attacked by drones on two consecutive days. Meanwhile, Russia's Defense Ministry reported downing 1,443 Ukrainian drones in two nights, surpassing the previous record. Strikes also hit Kyiv's bridges, killing two, and Ukraine targeted Russian industrial areas, including oil refineries in Ufa. Moscow reported 800 drones targeting the region, most intercepted. Germany and Norway pledged funding for U.S.-supplied air defense systems. Ukraine's Deputy Energy Minister noted power outages in nine regions due to Russian strikes on energy infrastructure. The attacks occurred as Russia and Ukraine await U.S.-mediated peace talks, which began with Moscow's invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.

item.title: El Dorado Arkansas Seeks to Correct Pronunciation Amid Travel Spotlight
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Arkansas city of El Dorado uses travel spotlight to clear its name. Call us ‘El Duh Ray Duh’
A system failure disrupted global air travel, linking a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, to the outage. The city of about 18,000 people used the attention to promote itself, correcting mispronunciations and highlighting local growth. The El Dorado-Union County Chamber of Commerce urged proper pronunciation as 'El Duh Ray Duh' or 'El Duh Ray Doe,' rejecting 'El Duh Rod Oh.' The chamber also promoted the city's 'El Duh Ray Duh Promise' for college tuition and tourism. Steven Jones, chamber president, noted companies like Standard Lithium are developing lithium projects near the city. The chamber capitalized on the situation to boost visibility, with Jones stating, 'We just thought why not capitalize on the marketing and have a little fun.'

item.title: AO3 Resumes Operations After Security Outage
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Fans cheer as AO3, a popular online platform for spinoff stories, nears full return after security incident
AO3, a fan-run platform for transformative works, resumed operations after a two-week outage beginning Oct. 29. A status update confirmed the site was back online, though features like user icons and external work imports remain disabled. The outage caused frustration among users, with some authors upset over unauthorized uploads to Google Drive during the downtime. The organization reported 2.6 million works and 2 million accounts, with user growth reaching 11 million registered users in June. Security experts speculate AI-enabled exploits may have contributed to the incident, though the cause remains unconfirmed. The group emphasized that user data and drafts were preserved but could not confirm if the database was compromised. Volunteers managing the site faced challenges in addressing security risks, with one expert noting the difficulty of content moderation at scale. Fans expressed relief at the platform's return, with users celebrating on social media. The site, which hosts fanfiction, fanart, and podfics, continues to grow despite ongoing concerns about content moderation and safety.

item.title: New Study: School Cellphone Bans Show Small Learning Gains, But Results Are Mixed
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: Do school cellphone bans work? New study says yes – but it's complicated
New research suggests school cellphone bans using locked pouches may improve math and reading scores by 1-2 weeks annually, according to a study by Harvard and Dartmouth researchers. The analysis of over 3 million students found statistically significant gains lasting up to three years, with Tom Kane of Harvard noting the benefits could accumulate over time. However, a separate April study by University of Michigan’s Brian Jacob found no meaningful achievement gains, though it did detect significant gains in high school math. The discrepancy stems from data methods: the new study used student-level NWEA test scores, while the April study averaged school-level results. Both studies tracked Yondr pouches, used in over 3,300 schools. Kane argues the cost ($25 per student) is justified by potential long-term benefits, while Stanford’s Tom Dee calls the findings disappointing and urges further research. The studies link declining test scores since 2013 to smartphone adoption, as smartphone access among teens rose from 25% in 2011 to 95% by 2018. Researchers now plan to study smartphone use outside school.

item.title: San Diego Ends Use of License Plate Readers and Smart Streetlights
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego, San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: San Diego City Council Ends Use of License Plate Readers and Smart Streetlights
San Diego City Council voted to end the city’s use of automated license plate readers and smart streetlight cameras, ending a three-year contract with Ubicquia and Flock. The unanimous decision terminates a $2 million annual agreement following public concerns over privacy and potential misuse. Mayor Todd Gloria will not veto the measure, acknowledging the council’s direction while stressing public safety. The move follows revelations that the technology was used to track a domestic violence victim linked to a former police officer. Police defended the use as part of an investigation into misconduct allegations. Council members cited growing public fear of technology overreach and civil rights risks, with Councilmember Kent Lee noting residents are 'more fearful than ever' of breaches. The decision reflects broader national concerns about government surveillance, including fears of federal data access. San Diego Police Chief Scott Wahl said operations will continue without the cameras. Critics warn the technology could be exploited for immigration enforcement. The council’s action aligns with a city ordinance requiring annual reviews of surveillance tech. Several members, including Stephan Whitburn, shifted positions due to community concerns. The removal of cameras, which captured 4 million vehicles monthly, will occur within 24 hours at no cost to the city.
item.source: ABC 10News San Diego, San Diego Union-Tribune

item.title: Former Brick By Brick Space to Host New Venue The Chevelle
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Original headline: Former Brick By Brick space already hosting new tenants
The former Brick By Brick venue in San Diego, closed in August 2023, is set to reopen as The Chevelle by December 4. Operators Geoff Davis and Nick Shores, members of local band Latex Grenade, plan live music events featuring metal, punk, EDM, and sports-themed shows. Upgrades include synchronized laser lights. Nearby Bull’s Smokin’ BBQ is also leasing space. Promoter Sulo King notes the building was sold in 2013 and redevelopment plans include the entire strip, including the Pechanga Sports Arena and SOMA strip mall. Brick By Brick originated as the Spirit of ’76 in 1976, later evolving into a metal hub with acts like Megadeth and Blue Oyster Cult. Jordan Mancino, who co-founded As I Lay Dying, retains the name and liquor license, seeking a new location. King reflects on challenges of finding property, citing his own studio’s redevelopment into Crack Shack. He acknowledges the decline of historic venues but notes the stress of maintaining old buildings. Mancino aims to replicate SOMA’s model of relocating rather than demolishing.

item.title: Voyager 1 Reaches Light-Day Distance from Earth
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth
NASA's Voyager 1, launched in 1977, has traveled a light-day from Earth, covering 26 billion kilometers in 49 years, two months, and 11 days. The spacecraft now travels at 61,000 km/h, aided by gravitational slingshots from Jupiter and Saturn. It took a historic portrait of the solar system from beyond Neptune in 1990. Voyager 1 will pass by Gliese 445, 17 light-years away, in about 40,000 years. It continues sending data from unexplored space, per JPL managers Suzanne Dodd and Kareem Badaruddin. The probe carries the Golden Record, a phonographic message containing sounds and languages, including a controversial recording of former UN Secretary-General Kurt Waldheim. Waldheim's voice was included despite his wartime past as a German officer, which surfaced after the spacecraft's launch.

item.title: USS Theodore Roosevelt arrives in Middle East amid Iran tensions
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: El USS Theodore Roosevelt, con base en San Diego, llega a Oriente Medio
The USS Theodore Roosevelt, based in San Diego, arrived in the Middle East, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington as part of a U.S. military show of force. The deployment comes amid President Donald Trump’s uncertainty over next steps in the Iran conflict, with Trump oscillating between threatening large-scale attacks and claiming the war is effectively over. The Roosevelt, accompanied by escort ships, joins a fleet of 13 destroyers, two cruisers, and a coastal combat vessel in the Arabian Sea, with additional ships in the Red Sea. The move follows midterm election losses for Trump’s party, partly due to public opposition to the Iran war. Trump warned Iran’s forces are ready to strike but said major attacks are unlikely. Meanwhile, the Strait of Hormuz remains a flashpoint, with Iranian-backed forces accusing U.S.-backed shipping routes of being dangerous due to mines. Six oil tankers have been damaged, and a projectile struck a vessel in the strait, causing fires. The U.S. military has redirected 150 merchant ships and disabled five since June under a naval blockade, reducing traffic through the strait to less than a third of pre-war levels.

item.title: Teen Rescued After Being Swept by Waves in La Jolla
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: Good Samaritans rush to rescue teen swept into dangerous surf off La Jolla
A teenager was swept into dangerous surf off La Jolla, Calif., after a wave knocked him from a rock. Mike Lin Ferrari, a surfer, witnessed the incident and described how the teen was initially carried out to sea before being pulled back toward rocks. A group of surfers, bystanders, and an off-duty lifeguard joined the rescue, with Ferrari and another man pulling the teen from the water. The teen suffered cuts and was unresponsive before being carried to emergency responders. San Diego Lifeguard Chief Daniel Orloff reported 22 rescues over the weekend, attributing the dangerous conditions to El Niño and warning of higher king tides through November 28. Orloff emphasized vigilance near shorelines, noting waves could breach bluffs and boardwalks. A separate incident involved a lifeguard taking 10 large waves on the head while rescuing a swimmer near La Jolla Cove.
